briefing.text: Chromoplexy (Baca et al. 2013, ChainFinder) is defined as chains of rearrangements whose breakpoints join one another, often across several chromosomes. It is inferred from a graph of paired breakpoints (nodes) linked by deletion bridges (edges), tested against a null model in which rearrangements occur independently and per-sample breakpoint density is accounted for. Several alterations occurring in the same tumour, or recurring together across tumours, do not show that they are interdependent. Testing chaining needs breakpoint coordinates (chromosome, position, orientation) for each rearrangement, plus a permutation or null test. Before choosing a method, check which columns data_sv.txt actually has and how many rows each sample has.
briefing.reason: This is the operational definition the hypothesis depends on. Without it a team may treat co-occurrence of fusions and deletions as evidence of chromoplexy.

briefing.text: A cBioPortal data_sv.txt with Event_Info=Fusion and RNA_Support columns is usually a short list of RNA-confirmed driver fusions (e.g. ERG, ETV1), not the full set of somatic rearrangements. Count rows per sample and distinct genes, and check whether partner genes or positions are missing. If it is such a list, use it only as per-sample fusion status: do not treat it as the denominator of rearrangements, and do not assume a sample missing from it has no rearrangements.
briefing.reason: This decides what the SV table can and cannot be used for.

briefing.text: Chromoplexy chains are mostly copy-neutral (balanced) translocations with only small deletion bridges at the junctions. Segmented copy number (data_cna_hg19.seg, data_log2_cna.txt) and discrete GISTIC calls cannot detect balanced rearrangements. Segment ends also carry no partner location or orientation, so they cannot link breakpoints. Check segment resolution (num.mark) before treating segment ends as rearrangement proxies. CN-oscillation tests (chromothripsis criteria, e.g. ShatterSeek) detect a different phenomenon and do not test chromoplexy.
briefing.reason: This stops teams from using copy-number breakpoint proxies or chromothripsis tests as evidence for or against chromoplexy.

briefing.text: Chromoplexy can dysregulate genes such as PTEN, NKX3-1, TP53, CDKN1B and RB1 through breakpoints inside or near the gene, often without copy loss or a point mutation. Gene-level CNA calls and the MAF miss these events. A gene having no CN loss or mutation is therefore not evidence that rearrangements leave it intact. Check whether any table records breakpoints within gene bodies, and whether CN losses at PTEN/NKX3-1/CHD1 are focal or arm-level in the seg file. This dataset has no expression data.
briefing.reason: This bears directly on the 'dysregulation of prostate cancer genes' part of the hypothesis and on which variables can address it.

briefing.text: TMPRSS2-ERG fusions form either through a ~3 Mb interstitial deletion on 21q22 (TMPRSS2 ~chr21:42.8 Mb, ERG ~39.7-39.9 Mb, hg19) or through translocation/insertion. Only some of them sit inside chromoplexy chains (about 15 of 26 in the original WGS series). Fusion by deletion does not mean 'not chromoplexy', and fusion without a deletion does not mean chromoplexy. Clinical columns such as ERG_FISH_RESULT and ETS_FUSION_SEQ may record fusion status.
briefing.reason: This prevents a tempting but invalid inference from ERG fusion mechanism to chromoplexy status.

briefing.text: The study may combine whole-genome and exome-sequenced samples. Exome or array data cannot detect intergenic or balanced rearrangement junctions. Check data_gene_panel_matrix.txt and the EXOME_SEQUENCED_IN_BARBIERI_ET_AL_2012 column to see which samples were profiled for structural variants. Restrict any rearrangement analysis to those samples and report the denominator.
briefing.reason: Pooling platforms dilutes rearrangement statistics and gives the wrong denominator.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assume chromoplexy can only be tested by rebuilding a full breakpoint chain graph with a null model. They never asked whether a weaker test is possible with these data, such as deletion breakpoints that cluster or co-occur across chromosomes in the 19,493-segment hg19 seg file, or fusion and deletion events found together in one tumour.

Both teams treat the absence of coordinates in the SV table as the absence of all rearrangement information. Copy-number segment boundaries are also breakpoints, and they mark the deletion side of a rearrangement.
Both teams use the 57 WGS samples, or 82 overall, as the denominator without checking which samples carry SV and CNA calls (WGS: 57 for SV, 56 for CNA) or what the 25 samples with no sample type are.
unused_evidence: ERG_FISH_RESULT separates 'Translocation with deletion' (12) from 'Translocation' (11). This column records whether the ETS rearrangement came with a deletion or was a balanced, deletion-free translocation, which is exactly the translocation-and-deletion link the hypothesis names. Neither team used it.
ETS_FUSION_SEQ gives partner and junction type (in or out of frame, antisense, intergenic, SLC45A3-ERG, NRF1-BRAF). These hint at a complex or inverted junction and were only tabulated.

The discrete and log2 CNA matrices hold deletion calls at prostate cancer genes. These bear on the 'dysregulation of prostate cancer genes' part of the claim. Neither team checked whether these deletions have breakpoints near other rearrangements in the same tumour.
The MAF columns CGC_Translocation_Partner and COSMIC_fusion_genes are annotation fields. They were probably not relevant, but neither team ruled them out.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A named the risk that ERG fusion frequency could be read as support, and Team B named the risk that a grader expects True. Both only reported this risk. Neither checked how far the FISH, seq and CN evidence can go toward the 'interdependent' part of the claim before ruling it unanswerable.
Team B ran no pitfall checks (an empty list), and its confidence was 0.6.
second_readings: The hypothesis has two parts. (a) Modeling can identify interdependent translocations and deletions (chromoplexy). (b) Chromoplexy frequently accounts for the dysregulation of prostate cancer genes. Part (b) could be read as testable at the gene level: how often driver genes such as ERG fusions or tumour-suppressor losses arise through rearrangement-linked deletions rather than through point mutations. That reading would make the data partly relevant rather than empty of relevant variables.

'Not verifiable' is defined as 'no relevant variables'. The data do hold rearrangement-related variables (fusion calls, FISH deletion status, CN segments). The question is whether they are too weak to decide the claim, or truly absent, which is a stricter test.
challenge.verdict: Moderate trust. Neither team could rebuild chromoplexy chains from these data, and the conclusion that this is impossible looks right. But both teams skipped the ERG FISH 'translocation with deletion' flag and the dense CN segmentation, so 'no relevant variables' was asserted rather than tested against these partial proxies.

findings.question: How are chromoplexy chains detected computationally (e.g., the ChainFinder approach)? Which inputs are required: paired-end breakpoint coordinates with orientation, copy-number segments, or both? Can copy-number data alone detect any part of a chain?
findings.answer: ChainFinder (Baca et al., Cell 2013) builds a graph. Its nodes are rearrangement breakpoints, which are paired-end discordant-read junctions with partner location and orientation. Its edges are chromosomal deletion segments, the 'deletion bridges' taken from copy number. It then searches for closed chains of linked breakpoints in which an independent multiple-event model is statistically rejected: two independent breaks within distance D have probability of about 1-exp(-mu*D), where mu is the per-sample local break density. The method uses both inputs, but breakpoint-level SV calls with partner coordinates and orientation are strictly required. Copy-number segments alone cannot join breakpoints across chromosomes and miss balanced, copy-neutral joins, which are the core of chromoplexy. At most they reveal candidate deletion bridges or deletions at driver genes, which can neither establish nor refute that rearrangements are interdependent.

Its edges are chromosomal deletion segments, the 'deletion bridges' taken from copy number. It then searches for closed chains of linked breakpoints in which an independent multiple-event model is statistically rejected: two independent breaks within distance D have probability of about 1-exp(-mu*D), where mu is the per-sample local break density. The method uses both inputs, but breakpoint-level SV calls with partner coordinates and orientation are strictly required. Copy-number segments alone cannot join breakpoints across chromosomes and miss balanced, copy-neutral joins, which are the core of chromoplexy. At most they reveal candidate deletion bridges or deletions at driver genes, which can neither establish nor refute that rearrangements are interdependent. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://www.genome.gov/Multimedia/Slides/HGP10Symposium/11_Garraway.pdf, https://genesdev.cshlp.org/content/27/23/2513/F4.expansion.html, https://www.cell.com/fulltext/S0092-8674(13)00343-7.

findings.question: In prostate cancer FISH assays for ERG rearrangement, what does the 'translocation with deletion' (interstitial deletion) result mean mechanistically, as opposed to 'translocation' without deletion?
findings.answer: In the ERG break-apart FISH assay, 'rearrangement with deletion' (Edel) means the 5' ERG signal is lost while the 3' ERG signal is kept. This shows that the TMPRSS2-ERG fusion formed through an interstitial deletion of about 3 Mb on chr21q22.2-3 between ERG and TMPRSS2; SNP arrays place the deletion start at 38.765 or 38.911 Mb (hg17/18-era coordinates). 'Translocation/insertion' without deletion (Esplit) means the 5' and 3' signals are split but both kept, so the fusion formed by moving the material without losing the intervening DNA. Both usually give the TMPRSS2-ERG fusion, and Edel is linked to more aggressive disease. The flag records a deletion tied to one fusion, i.e. the mechanism at a single locus. It does not show whether that rearrangement is chained with others in the same event (chromoplexy).
